method: results-blind operational measurement on this host: per-worker CPU and RSS sampled from the live production runners during startup. Only timing/utilization telemetry was read; no scientific outcome field was inspected to choose this number.
why_not_higher: Measured demand is 1.51 logical cores per worker, not 1.0 -- PySR runs parallelism='serial' (required by deterministic=True) but the process is not strictly single-threaded (Julia runtime/GC and the classifier's SIMPLIFY_TIMEOUT child process both add load). 16 workers would demand 16 x 1.51 = 24.2 logical cores, i.e. full saturation, and 24 workers would demand ~36 -- severe oversubscription. The ARM host's own history records exactly this failure mode: an oversubscription episode reaching load average 63, and later 111, when too many shards were run (E2_EXECUTION_DEVIATION.md sections 10f, 14).
why_not_lower: 9 workers would leave roughly 30% of logical capacity idle with no safety benefit; memory is nowhere near a constraint at 25%.
consistency_with_prior_host: The ARM host measured per-worker CPU of 117-165%. This host measures 151%, inside that band -- the execution profile is the same, so the same conservative sizing logic applies, rescaled to this topology.
scientific_inertness: Worker count cannot affect any result: seed_val = seed_base + world_ordinal * seeds_per_world + k depends only on world identity, and shard assignment is world_ordinal % n_shards, so no seed, budget, or classification depends on how many shards run. Verified in source before launch.
shard_balance: 540 worlds / 12 shards = exactly 45 worlds per shard

steady_state_measurement.measured_after: all 12 shards up, staggered 12s apart to avoid a simultaneous Julia JIT storm
steady_state_measurement.concurrent_processes: 23-24 (12 shard parents + their SIMPLIFY_TIMEOUT classifier children)
steady_state_measurement.interpretation: near-full utilisation with LOW system time. 89% user vs 5.5% sys means the machine is doing real work, not thrashing on scheduling. The elevated run queue is what saturation looks like when many runnable processes share cores, not a pathology.

first_launch_incident.what_happened: the first launch started all 12 shards simultaneously; 12 concurrent Julia JIT compilations drove load to 87-112 with a run queue of 40-145
first_launch_incident.diagnosis: startup transient, not steady-state demand. Verified directly: at rest a worker has Threads.nthreads()=1, Threads.ngcthreads()=1 and only 2 OS threads, so Julia thread pools were not the cause
first_launch_incident.resolution: stopped the run while 0 worlds and 0 candidate rows had been written (nothing lost), cleared the partial cache, relaunched with 12s-staggered starts
first_launch_incident.scientific_impact: none -- no world record, candidate row, or cache entry from the aborted launch survived

ab_test_not_run_and_why.intended: compare measured throughput at 12 shards vs 8 shards and keep the faster
ab_test_not_run_and_why.not_run_because: the persistent classify cache warms monotonically as the run proceeds, so a later sample benefits from a warmer cache regardless of shard count. Any sequential A/B on a single run is confounded by cache warming and would systematically favour whichever configuration is measured second. Running the two arms concurrently is impossible (they would contend for the same host).
ab_test_not_run_and_why.conclusion: 12 retained. At 12 shards the host is already at ~94% logical-CPU occupancy with only 5.5% system time; 8 shards would run ~16 processes on 24 logical cores and leave roughly a third of the machine idle. Going above 12 would add processes to an already-saturated machine.
ab_test_not_run_and_why.honesty_note: this is a resource-utilisation argument, not a measured throughput comparison; it is not claimed to be one.
